children.gist: Embryos and adults differ in structure within the same class, yet some animals like cuttlefish and spiders show no metamorphosis at all, raising the question of why embryonic resemblance across species is common but not universal.

children.title: Timing and inheritance of variation
children.gist: Variations in offspring need not first appear early in life but can be triggered before formation of the embryo and yet manifest late, and such variations tend to reappear in offspring at the same age at which they appeared in the parent.

children.title: Applying the two principles to species
children.gist: Applying the principle that modifications appear and are inherited at corresponding later ages explains why embryos of related species resemble one another far more than the adults do, since limbs destined to become hands, paddles, or wings start out alike.

children.title: Embryo as picture of ancestor
children.gist: Because embryos represent organisms in their less modified ancestral state, embryonic resemblance across species reveals shared descent, so classifying by embryo structure is more reliable than classifying by the more specialized adult form.

children.title: Rudimentary organs
children.gist: Rudimentary organs—like useless mammary glands in male mammals, unerupted teeth in whale and cattle fetuses, and flightless wings in beetles—are widespread in nature and plainly correspond to functional organs in related forms.

children.title: Disuse explains rudimentary organs
children.gist: Disuse across generations, sometimes aided by natural selection against a harmful organ, gradually reduces structures to uselessness, and because reduction typically occurs at maturity, inheritance at corresponding ages keeps rudimentary organs relatively larger in embryos than in adults.

children.title: Summary
children.gist: Darwin summarizes that nested classification, nonarbitrary affinities, variable character values, morphology's shared body plans, embryonic resemblance, and rudimentary organs all follow naturally from common descent modified by natural selection, extinction, and divergence.

children.title: Concluding reflection
children.gist: Darwin concludes that the facts of classification, morphology, embryology, and rudimentary organs together so strongly indicate common ancestry that he would accept descent with modification even without any other supporting evidence.

children.title: CHAPTER XIV. RECAPITULATION AND CONCLUSION
children.gist: Weighing the difficulties against the converging evidence, Darwin concludes that descent with modification through natural selection best explains life's history and unity, ennobling rather than diminishing our view of nature.
children.question: Recapitulation and conclusion — on balance, does descent through natural selection outweigh its difficulties as the explanation of life's diversity? (final weighing of evidence)

children.title: Recapitulation introduced
children.gist: Darwin introduces his final chapter by promising to briefly recapitulate the whole book's leading facts and inferences, since the volume forms one continuous argument.

children.title: Difficulties restated
children.gist: Darwin reviews the gravest objections—missing gradations, sterile worker ants, hybrid sterility versus variety fertility, puzzling geographic distribution, and the fossil record's lack of transitional links—and argues each stems from ignorance rather than disproving descent with modification.

children.title: Variation and struggle for existence
children.gist: Domestic variability shows that disturbed reproductive systems produce heritable change, which breeders then select, and since wild nature shows similar variability plus a constant struggle for existence from overpopulation, natural selection should likewise act there.

children.title: Facts explained by the theory
children.gist: Many otherwise puzzling facts—blurred species boundaries, divergence into groups, odd animal adaptations, imperfect contrivances, variable specific versus stable generic characters, graded instincts, and hybrid crossing patterns—become intelligible once species are seen as descended varieties rather than independent creations.

children.title: Geological succession supports descent
children.gist: Given an extremely imperfect fossil record, the patterns we do find—gradual appearance of species, extinction following competition, non-reappearance of lost forms, intermediate fossil character, and long persistence of related forms on one continent—all fit descent with modification rather than independent creation.

children.title: Geographical distribution supports descent
children.gist: Past migration driven by climatic and geographic change, combined with gradual modification, explains striking patterns in distribution—parallel geological and geographic relatedness, sparse peculiar island faunas limited to capable dispersers, and islands resembling their nearest mainland source.

children.title: Affinities, morphology, embryology, rudiments
children.gist: Shared skeletal plans across very different limbs, embryonic resemblance among vertebrate classes, and the persistence of useless rudimentary organs like a calf's unerupted teeth all point to common descent rather than separate creation, since natural selection and disuse act mainly on mature, not embryonic, structures.

children.title: Why naturalists resist mutability
children.gist: Darwin argues that naturalists reject mutability mainly from habit and an inability to grasp vast timescales, not from genuine proof, noting that scientists who admit some species are secondary variations illogically insist others must be separately and miraculously created.

children.title: How far the theory extends
children.gist: Darwin argues the theory likely applies to whole classes descended from only four or five animal progenitors and a similar few plant ones, and by analogy perhaps all life from one primordial form, predicting this view will transform classification, terminology, and the broader excitement of natural history study.

children.title: Effects on the study of natural history
children.gist: Geology's fossil record, though a poor and incomplete sample rather than a full museum, can still serve as a rough gauge of elapsed time once we recognize that organic change is driven by competing organisms rather than sudden catastrophes or miraculous creation.

children.title: Concluding remarks
children.gist: Darwin closes by predicting insight into psychology and human origins, arguing that viewing species as descended rather than separately created is more noble and consistent with natural law, and famously likens life's diversity to an entangled bank where simple laws of growth, inheritance, variation, and struggle have produced endless beautiful forms.
